The Story of Parshuram

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who carries beings across the ocean of existence, and I write the story of Parshuram, which inspires wonder.

King Kartavirya of Ayodhya was utterly foolish. His queen was Padmavati. In the forest of Ayodhya, there was an ashram of an ascetic named Yamdagni. The ascetic's wife was Renuka. They had two sons — Shvetram and Mahendrarām. One day, Renuka's brother, the monk Vardatt, came that way. He stopped under a tree. Seeing him, Renuka came with great love to meet him, joined her hands, and sat beside him. The wise monk Vardatt said to her, "Sister, I shall teach you some dharma. Listen carefully. All living beings desire happiness, but few seek true happiness, and that is why most people are miserable. The cause of true happiness is acquiring pure right faith. Those who attain right faith do not wander in lower births. Their cycle of existence diminishes, and many attain liberation in this very life.

"The ordinary form of right faith is this: faith in the true God, the true Guru, and the true Scripture. The true God is one who is free from the eighteen faults — hunger, thirst, attachment, aversion, anger, greed, pride, deceit, and more — whose knowledge is so vast that no thing in the universe remains unknown, who is worshipped even by the gods of heaven, Vidyadharas, Chakravartins, and great kings, and whose sacred teaching brings happiness in this world and the next. The nature of dharma is known through its ten marks — supreme forgiveness, supreme gentleness, supreme honesty, and so on. And the true Guru is one who observes conduct and restraint, whose life's purpose is the practice of knowledge and meditation, and who has not even a particle of attachment. Faith in these is called right faith. Besides this, for householders, giving to worthy recipients, worshipping the Lord, observing the lesser vows, the supplementary vows, and the rules of conduct, and fasting on holy days — these too are essential."

Hearing this discourse, Renuka's mind was transformed. She abandoned the worship of false gods and took faith in Jain dharma. Through the power of right faith, she eventually attained liberation.

Her sons Shvetram and Mahendrarām, however, did not follow the path of dharma. Mahendrarām, in particular, became violent and wrathful. He took up arms and killed many who opposed him. He became known as Parshuram — "Rama with the axe" — for his fierce nature. Through his violence, he accumulated heavy sins and suffered greatly in lower births. Eventually, through the ripening of merit, he regained human form, remembered his past folly, and turned to the path of non-violence and compassion. He practised austerities and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that right faith is the foundation of all spiritual progress. Without it, even those born in holy families can fall into violence and suffering. But with right faith, even the most fallen can rise to the highest goal. The wise should cultivate faith in the true God, Guru, and Scripture, and follow the path of dharma with sincerity.
